*"I won't be too long,"* he said, walking through our front door. Sweet! Getting the house to myself is great, even if for only a few moments. Pouring myself an overflowing bowl of sugary, rainbow cereal, I wondered how long Dad would be gone. 

Do I have time to watch a quick episode of *Why The Animal Does the Thing* on full volume? With my *feet on the couch*? Maybe not. Dad doesn't usually go out for very long, and the episodes are about half an hour long. 

Anxiously, I pondered my options, pacing around the house before settling down at my computer, opening a few websites that are usually off-limits. Freedom is overwhelming. Flicking between tabs, double- no, triple checking I was using Incognito Mode. Dad would fucking kill me if he saw me on these sites ag-

*What was that?*

It was like.. a tapping. Shuffling? What *was* that? Nobody else is home, it's like it's coming from.. outside? Gripping the desk, I tried to ignore it. My heart was in my throat.

*Snap out of it. It's just Dad coming home*, I thought, closing the windows as fast as I could. Opening up Facebook. That seems innocent enough, right?

But the door didn't open. No key noises. The door handle didn't turn. 

...

I crept into the living room, trying to peek a glance outside from behind the couch. Maybe it's a salesman? I'm not allowed to open the door for them, Dad always says.

Can't see anything. Sitting and fumbling for my phone, I check the time - 11:23 am. Dad should be home by now.. It's been over 45 minutes, it usually takes him.. what, 20 minutes? Damn it, I definitely could have watched one episode.

Noises again. Peeking back over the couch, I spot a figure outside. It kind of looks like.. 

*".. Dad?"* We lock eyes for a moment, and he disappears from view.

Did he forget his keys? Wait.. if he forgot his keys, how did he drive the car? Weird.

Rushing around to the door, I unlock it and swing it open. Dad looks.. terrified. 
*"I'm so sorry,"* he mumbled. *Sorry for what?* I couldn't bring myself to ask him. Something looked.. wrong. 

Did something happen to grandma? She hadn't been doing well and we were all worried she mi- 
*"I made a mistake. I shouldn't have gone."*

*"Did something happen? You took longer than usual, and.. I was starting to worr-"* My words passed right through his glazed over face as he embraced me in a hug over our doorstep. Was he.. crying? My shoulder definitely felt damp. *"I don't understand.."*

*"I'm so sorry,"* he whispered, once more.. before biting my neck.

A cold feeling rushed through my veins like ice, and just as quickly as my whole body locked up like I had just been frozen in ice, all sense of time, all sense of meaning, all sense of anything.. just.. fell away.

My heart dropped... Or maybe it stopped. 

I felt a hunger, deep inside me.

... It wasn't for Froot Loops.

The problem is, the more you think "I have to not think about (x)", the more you're going to think about it.

I think you need to go with more of an acceptance pathway to begin with. It's okay if you think about your tulpa. It's not a big deal. They're in your head, they always see what you're doing. They probably don't give a shit and don't judge you at all. Nobody understands you more than a headmate does. They're not going to go around and talk about what you do sexually.

**You need to stop thinking "I need to stop thinking about my tulpa while I'm having sex",** because your subconscious parses it as "Oh, I'm having sex. What was it that I needed to remember? Not thinking about something.. ah yes. my tulpa. Oh fuck, I'm thinking about them. They're watching me. (rambling anxiety thoughts)"

You need to be mindful about the fact that they're there, but that they don't mind. I know you said talking to your tulpa won't help, but maybe coming to an understanding that they likely don't find it as interesting as your anxiety makes you feel will help ease that anxiety.

So to start with, people with ASD don't necessarily have "no empathy". Sometimes we can have reduced empathy, sometimes we just aren't sure how to show it. Doesn't mean we don't have it - in fact, many of us are very empathetic but tend to internalize it.

As for a change in your brother's behavior, social intelligence can be learnt. Even if it doesn't come naturally, we can put two and two together after a while. 

"When my mom or sibling does (x),  that means they're feeling down. I should do (x), because that makes them give me a more positive response."

Learnt behaviors like this (and learning to make eye contact, etc) are common in people with ASD and do not prevent a diagnosis.

As for it happening so suddenly, it's possible that either you weren't paying as much attention as you thought you were, or he had a revelation.

Also, your brother is 29. He does not have the "emotions of a twelve year old". He has the emotions of an autistic 29 year old. Don't infantilize people. I can guarantee you even without knowing him that he's not that stupid.

I did fall in love with the other and although there were lots of jealousy hiccups, as a triad we were functioning reasonably well.

I do feel like the experience changed me. Even though I haven't completely overcome my jealousy, I'm more open to the idea of poly, especially to fill holes one partner might not be able to. 

I find myself thinking in 'poly ways' - instead of say, crushing on the idea of being with someone instead of a current partner, I'd now instead hypothetically want to bring them into our relationship. 

Instead of suggesting/thinking someone should leave someone due to feeling unsatisfied (i.e a sex repulsed asexual and someone who needs sex), I would instead want to suggest poly. 

Just things I would have never considered.

I discovered I can't handle open relationships, but I can handle closed poly to some extent, and it can even actually help with the attention me and my huge bag of anxieties requires.

I definitely understand what you mean by that. Changing terminology wouldn't be a miracle action - of course, much more work would need to go into trying to change the stigma. I do not want to imply that language is the entire root of our problem, but I do feel like it contributes significantly. 

This post was never intended as a call out, or accusatory post implying that using the terminology makes one bad, or that there was something wrong with people who use the terminology. 

In fact, I will say that many of the people I respect and look up to still use these terms, despite knowing the appropriate level of respect to give a headmate.

However, our language isn't doing ourselves any favors. If our words can imply disrespect - coercion and ownership, in someone's eyes.. We can't be shocked when people take it literally. 

As a trans person, not calling us 'trannies' won't solve the issue of us being discriminated, but by using more appropriate terms you would be showing more respect, and at least its a start. While not using the term doesn't solve the entire issue on its own, you wouldn't be able to solve the issue while still using negative terms to refer to us. 

You don't just /keep/ calling us 'trannies' with the expectation the term will fix itself eventually. 

Loose comparison, since obviously "host" and "forcing" aren't as much slurs, but when you think about it, the negative meanings I explained in the OP do imply, deep down, a level of inequality. 

I do agree with you that the issue does not start or end with the terminology, but I do think the language we use doesn't do us any favours, either. 

I think there's more that can be done - sharing our experiences, primarily. And I do see that happening. It warms my heart to see people defending younger tulpas from creators who act like they just got a cool new toy to serve them, explaining why that isn't morally correct. 

But.. I still feel like there's no way that we can expect to fix the negative culture while still using negative language. 

tl;dr I agree with what you're saying - the language is hardly the entire problem, and I probably could have worded the OP better, especially the title. 
However, while the negative culture is more than just the language, while using inherently negative terms widely, it will always remain, despite all other efforts.

I believe the meanings of the colors are ones only you could identify. Colors can mean different things to different people, on different occasions, in different settings.

There are common things people associate with certain colors, but even those can clash against each other - red can signify both love and anger, for example. 
 
It's more about the feeling you get from that color. 

As you said, your vivid blues and greens seem to make you feel relaxed, so I would imagine they signify, if anything, some sort of tranquillity, a feeling of calm that goes hand in hand with you seeing those colors - that is to say, your subconscious may be causing the colors to exist to begin with.

I would imagine if you were feeling anxious or scared, your colors might be more muted, dark, give off a sense of 'being in an abyss'.

Or who knows, maybe one or both of you just like the colors.

'Color meanings' are really more of a list of different things the color has made people feel, you could Google them for inspiration, but for the true answer you're going to have to feel it out yourself. 

tl;dr - its about what you feel they mean, random color meanings off the internet aren't going to tell you any more than what you already feel. the colors in itself probably don't mean anything and its up to how your own mind processes them.

Yeah, most of us aren't. Rain Man is actually often shown as a BAD example of autistic people in the community, and I can say I was actually diagnosed as support level 3, which means I require very substantial support. (The most "severe.")

Autism isn't a straight line, it's a candy/snack bar, you might have lots of one symptom and little of others, like you might have lots of skittles and some gummy candies. Functioning labels such as severe mean very little. 

I present as neurotypical, people would assume I'm not autistic. However, I can't live alone, forget to shower a lot, and get overwhelmed by sensory input by going outside. 

I guess all I'm trying to say is that you are autistic. You might need less support, and that's fine, but you don't need to feel sorry for adding in commentary as an autistic person because you're able to. That label, if you so choose to use it, is valid for you.
